capstone.brief: Keep clean books for a real small business for 30 days. Record every sale and cost, keep every receipt, reconcile the bank, and produce a real income statement and balance sheet at the end.
checks: Books set up with a clear chart of accounts
capstone.title: Keep Clean Books for a Real Business for 30 Days

course.tagline: Keep clean business books: income, expenses and reports a business can trust.
course.title: Bookkeeping Basics

days.challenge: Explain bookkeeping to a friend using a market trader example, in 30 seconds.
days.goal: Explain what bookkeeping is and why a business needs it.

quiz.explain: Bookkeeping means writing down every sale and every cost, so a business knows its money.
options: Writing down every sale and cost, so a business knows its money
quiz.q: What is bookkeeping?

quiz.explain: Clean books show profit, stop money leaking, and make tax time easy.
options: Clean books are only for big companies
Clean books show profit, stop leaks, and make tax easy
Books are only for the bank
Books do not matter if you sell well
quiz.q: Why does a business need clean books?

quiz.explain: Bookkeeping records the money. Accounting uses those records to make reports and decisions.
options: Bookkeeping records money, accounting uses the records for reports
quiz.q: What is the difference between bookkeeping and accounting?

steps: Watch the video and write what bookkeeping means in your own words.
Think of a market trader who writes each sale in a notebook. That is bookkeeping.
Write down three things clean books help a business do.
Pick a small business you know and guess what its books look like.
Write down one thing you want to learn in 30 days.
Write one sentence about why clean books matter.
days.task: Write a short note explaining bookkeeping, with three ways it helps a business.
days.title: What Bookkeeping Is

video.title: ACCOUNTING BASICS: Debits and Credits Explained

days.challenge: Work out what a shop owns if it has 100,000 in assets and owes 40,000.
days.goal: Understand the accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.

quiz.explain: Assets are what the business owns. Liabilities are what it owes. Equity is what is left for the owner.
options: Assets are debts, liabilities are cash
Assets are what it owns, liabilities what it owes, equity what is left
Assets and liabilities are the same
quiz.q: What are assets, liabilities and equity?

quiz.explain: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Both sides must always balance.
quiz.q: What is the accounting equation?

quiz.explain: If assets are 100,000 and liabilities are 40,000, equity is 60,000.
quiz.q: A shop has 100,000 in assets and owes 40,000. What is its equity?

steps: Write down the equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.
List three assets a small shop owns: cash, stock, equipment.
List two liabilities: a loan and money owed to a supplier.
Work out the equity with your own numbers.
Write down one example where the equation stays balanced after a sale.
Keep the equation on a card next to your notes.
days.task: Write the accounting equation with a real example from a small shop.
days.title: The Accounting Equation

video.title: Complete Accounting Cycle: From Journal Entries to Balance Sheet

days.challenge: Work out the debit and credit for buying stock with cash.
days.goal: Understand debits and credits in plain words.

quiz.explain: A debit adds to assets and costs. A credit adds to what the business owes and to income.
options: Debit and credit are the same
A debit adds to assets and costs, a credit adds to debts and income
A debit always means less money
A credit always means less money
quiz.q: What do debit and credit mean?

quiz.explain: Every transaction has a debit and a credit of the same amount, so the books stay balanced.
options: Every transaction has a debit and a credit of the same amount
quiz.q: Why does every transaction have two sides?

quiz.explain: When you sell for cash, you debit cash and credit sales income.
quiz.q: You sell goods for cash. What do you record?

steps: Write down the simple rule: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.
Work out one example: you buy stock with cash. Debit stock, credit cash.
Work out a second: you sell goods for cash. Debit cash, credit sales.
Work out a third: you pay rent. Debit rent cost, credit cash.
Write all three examples in your notes.
Say each one out loud until it feels simple.
days.task: Write three debit and credit examples: buying stock, selling goods, paying rent.
days.title: Debits and Credits in Plain Words

video.title: Accounting For Beginners #1 / Debits and Credits / Assets = Liabilities + Equity

days.challenge: Set up your books in a spreadsheet in under 30 minutes.
days.goal: Set up simple books for a small business.

quiz.explain: A bookkeeping system can be a spreadsheet or an app like Wave, as long as every transaction is recorded.
options: A spreadsheet or a free app works if every transaction is recorded
You must hire an accountant first
quiz.q: What do you need to keep books?

quiz.explain: Separate business money from personal money, so the books stay clean and honest.
quiz.q: Why keep business money separate from personal money?

quiz.explain: A good setup has accounts for sales, costs, cash, bank, and what is owed to and by the business.
options: A good setup has accounts for sales, costs, cash, bank and debts
Only a cash account is needed
Only a sales account is needed
quiz.q: What should your setup include?

steps: Pick a small business to keep books for: yours, a family business, or a pretend one.
Open a spreadsheet or a free app like Wave.
Make one sheet for sales and one for costs.
Add columns for date, what it was, amount, and receipt.
Open a separate bank account or wallet for the business if you can.
Write down your opening balances: cash, bank and stock.
days.task: Set up your books in a spreadsheet or free app, with sales and cost sheets.
days.title: Set Up Your Books

days.challenge: List every account your business needs, in five minutes.
days.goal: Build a chart of accounts: a list of all your bookkeeping buckets.

quiz.explain: A chart of accounts is a list of all the buckets where money is recorded: sales, costs, cash, bank, debts.
options: A list of all the buckets where money is recorded
quiz.q: What is a chart of accounts?

quiz.explain: Clear buckets make reports easy, because every naira or dollar sits in the right place.
options: Buckets are only for big companies
quiz.q: Why use a chart of accounts?

quiz.explain: Start small with the accounts you need, and add more only when you need them.
options: Start small, add accounts only when needed
Use the same list as a big company
quiz.q: How many accounts should a small business start with?

steps: Write five groups: assets, liabilities, equity, income and costs.
Under income, list your sales types.
Under costs, list rent, stock, transport, phone and other costs.
Under assets, list cash, bank and stock.
Under liabilities, list loans and money owed to suppliers.
Keep the list short: about 15 to 20 accounts is enough to start.
days.task: Write a chart of accounts with about 15 to 20 accounts in five groups.
days.title: Chart of Accounts

days.challenge: Record five transactions today, with a receipt for each one.
days.goal: Record your first transactions correctly.

quiz.explain: A transaction is any money movement: a sale, a cost, or a payment.
options: Any money movement: a sale, a cost, or a payment
quiz.q: What is a transaction?

quiz.explain: Record the date, what it was, the amount, and keep the receipt.
options: Date, what it was, amount, and keep the receipt
quiz.q: What should you record for each transaction?

quiz.explain: Recording daily keeps the books accurate and stops a pile of forgotten papers.
options: Recording once a year is fine
quiz.q: Why record transactions daily?

steps: Pick five real or pretend transactions for the business.
For each one, write the date, what it was, and the amount.
Put each one in the right bucket from your chart of accounts.
Write the debit and credit for each one.
Keep a receipt or a note for each transaction.
Check that your debits and credits balance.
days.task: Record five transactions with date, description, amount and receipt.
days.title: Record Your First Transactions

days.challenge: Show your books to a friend and ask if they can follow them.
days.goal: Put your setup, chart and first transactions together into clean books.

project.brief: Set up clean books for a small business: a chart of accounts, opening balances, and at least ten transactions recorded correctly with receipts. Someone else should be able to follow your books.
checks: Every transaction has a receipt or note
Books are neat enough for someone else to follow
project.title: Set Up Clean Books for a Small Business

quiz.explain: Clean books are complete, neat, and easy for someone else to follow.
options: Books that are complete, neat and easy to follow
quiz.q: What makes books clean?

quiz.explain: Opening balances are the starting amounts of cash, bank, stock and debts.
options: The starting amounts of cash, bank, stock and debts
quiz.q: What are opening balances?

quiz.explain: If someone else can follow your books, they are clear enough to trust.
options: If someone else can follow them, they are clear enough
Only you need to understand them
quiz.q: Why should someone else be able to follow your books?

steps: Check your chart of accounts is complete.
Check your opening balances are written down.
Record five more transactions so you have ten.
File every receipt with its transaction.
Check debits equal credits.
Ask a friend to look at your books and tell you what is unclear.
days.task: Finish your clean books setup with ten transactions and filed receipts.
days.title: Week 1 Project: Set Up Clean Books

days.challenge: Record today's sales before you sleep tonight.
days.goal: Record sales income correctly every day.

quiz.explain: Sales income is money earned from selling goods or services.
options: Money earned from selling goods or services
quiz.q: What is sales income?

quiz.explain: Record the sale on the day it happens, even if the buyer pays later.
options: Record it when the buyer pays
Record it on the day it happens
Record it only if paid in cash
quiz.q: When do you record a sale?

quiz.explain: Cash sales and credit sales are both income, but credit sales also create money owed to you.
options: Cash and credit sales are both income, but credit creates money owed to you
quiz.q: What is the difference between a cash sale and a credit sale?

steps: Write down every sale the business makes today.
For each sale, note the date, the item, the amount, and cash or credit.
If it is a credit sale, also note who owes the money and when they will pay.
Add up the day's sales at night.
Write the total in your sales sheet.
Check the total matches the cash you received plus what is owed.
days.task: Record all of today's sales with date, item, amount and cash or credit.
days.title: Record Sales Income

video.title: #6 / Putting an Asset on the Balance Sheet

days.challenge: Keep every receipt today, even for small buys.
days.goal: Record business costs correctly every day.

quiz.explain: A business cost is money spent to run the business, like stock, rent and transport.
options: Money spent to run the business
quiz.q: What is a business cost?

quiz.explain: Separate business costs from personal costs, or your profit will look wrong.
options: Separate them or your profit will look wrong
quiz.q: Why separate business and personal costs?

quiz.explain: Small costs add up, so record every cost, even a small one.
options: Small costs add up, so record every one
Costs under a limit can be skipped
quiz.q: Why record small costs too?

steps: Write down every cost the business has today.
For each cost, note the date, what it was for, and the amount.
Put each cost in the right bucket from your chart.
Keep the receipt for each cost.
Add up the day's costs at night.
Check that no personal spending slipped into the business books.
days.task: Record all of today's business costs with receipts.
days.title: Record Business Costs

days.challenge: Find one receipt from last week and file it properly.
days.goal: Keep receipts and proof for every transaction.

quiz.explain: A receipt is proof that a sale or a cost really happened, with the date and amount.
options: Proof of a sale or cost, with date and amount
quiz.q: What is a receipt?

quiz.explain: Receipts prove your books are true, help at tax time, and settle arguments.
options: Receipts are only for big buys
Receipts prove your books, help at tax time, settle arguments
quiz.q: Why keep receipts?

quiz.explain: A simple folder, one per month, keeps receipts easy to find.
options: A simple folder per month keeps receipts easy to find
A pile on a desk is fine
Receipts can be thrown away daily
quiz.q: How should you store receipts?

steps: Make a folder for this month's receipts, paper or digital.
Put today's receipts in it, one by one.
For each receipt, write the date and what it was for if it is not clear.
Take a photo of paper receipts as a backup.
At the end of the week, check every transaction has a receipt.
File any missing receipt by asking the seller for a copy.
days.task: Set up a receipt folder and file every receipt from this week.
days.title: Receipts and Proof

days.challenge: Compare your bank balance with your books today and find any difference.
days.goal: Reconcile your bank: match your books with your bank statement.

quiz.explain: Reconciling means comparing your books with your bank statement to find mistakes.
options: Comparing your books with your bank statement
quiz.q: What does reconciling mean?

quiz.explain: Small differences usually come from bank fees, missed entries or timing.
options: Bank fees, missed entries or timing
quiz.q: Why do books and bank statements differ?

quiz.explain: Monthly reconciliation catches errors early, before they grow.
options: Reconciling once a year is fine
quiz.q: Why reconcile every month?

steps: Get your bank statement for this month.
Write down your book balance for the bank account.
Compare the two numbers.
List every difference: bank fees, money not yet cleared, or missed entries.
Fix each difference in your books.
Write down your final reconciled balance and the date.
days.task: Reconcile your bank account for this month and list every difference.
days.title: Reconcile Your Bank

days.challenge: List everyone who owes your business money, with amounts and dates.
days.goal: Track accounts receivable: money customers owe you.

quiz.explain: Accounts receivable is money customers owe you for goods or services they took on credit.
options: Money customers owe you for credit sales
quiz.q: What is accounts receivable?

quiz.explain: A list of who owes you, how much, and when it is due helps you collect on time.
options: A list of who owes you, how much and when due helps you collect
quiz.q: Why track money owed to you?

quiz.explain: Send a polite reminder, then a firmer one, and agree a payment date.
options: Send a polite reminder, then firmer, agree a date
quiz.q: What do you do when a customer pays late?

steps: List every credit sale from your books.
For each one, write who owes you, how much, and the due date.
Add up the total owed to you.
Mark any that are overdue.
Send a polite reminder to anyone overdue.
Write down what you expect to collect this week.
days.task: Make a list of everyone who owes your business money, with amounts and due dates.
days.title: Money Owed to You

video.title: ACCOUNTING BASICS: Debits and Credits Explained

days.challenge: List everyone your business owes money to, with amounts and due dates.
days.goal: Track accounts payable: money you owe suppliers.

quiz.explain: Accounts payable is money you owe suppliers for goods or services you took on credit.
options: Money you owe suppliers for credit buys
quiz.q: What is accounts payable?

quiz.explain: A list of what you owe, to whom and when it is due stops late fees and lost trust.
options: A list of what you owe, to whom and when due stops late fees
You should forget what you owe
quiz.q: Why track money you owe?
What happens if you pay a supplier late?
options: You may pay late fees and lose trust
quiz.explain: Paying late can mean extra fees and a supplier who no longer trusts you.

steps: List every credit purchase from your books.
For each one, write who you owe, how much, and the due date.
Add up the total you owe.
Mark any that are due this week.
Plan which ones to pay first from your cash.
Write down your total owed and your cash available.
days.task: Make a list of everyone your business owes money to, with amounts and due dates.
days.title: Money You Owe

video.title: Complete Accounting Cycle: From Journal Entries to Balance Sheet

days.challenge: Record every transaction for three days in a row without missing one.
days.goal: Record a full week of real business transactions.

project.brief: Record one full week of real business transactions: every sale, every cost, every payment in and out. Keep every receipt, update your lists of money owed to you and by you, and check that debits equal credits at the end.
checks: Debits equal credits at week end
project.title: Record One Week of Real Transactions

quiz.explain: Missing one day breaks the chain and makes the books wrong.
options: Missing one day breaks the chain
quiz.q: Why record every day without gaps?
What should you do at the end of each week?
options: Check that every sale and cost is recorded
quiz.explain: A weekly check catches missing entries while you still remember them.

quiz.q: Why keep receipts with your records?
quiz.explain: Receipts prove what you spent and help you fix mistakes later.

steps: Record every sale and cost for seven days.
File every receipt the same day.
Update your owed-to-you and owed-by-you lists daily.
Each evening, check debits equal credits.
At the end of the week, add up total sales and total costs.
Write one sentence about what the week showed you.
days.task: Record seven full days of transactions with receipts and balanced books.
days.title: Week 2 Project: Record One Week

video.title: Accounting For Beginners #1 / Debits and Credits / Assets = Liabilities + Equity

days.challenge: Write a journal entry for buying stock on credit.
days.goal: Write journal entries: the first step in the accounting cycle.

quiz.explain: A journal entry is the first written record of a transaction, with its debit and credit.
options: The first written record of a transaction, with debit and credit
quiz.q: What is a journal entry?

quiz.explain: A journal entry has a date, a description, a debit account and amount, and a credit account and amount.
options: Date, description, debit account and amount, credit account and amount
quiz.q: What does a journal entry include?

quiz.explain: The journal is the first step. Later steps sort entries into accounts and reports.
options: The journal is the first step in the cycle
The journal is the last step
quiz.q: Where does the journal fit in the accounting cycle?

steps: Pick five transactions from your week.
For each one, write the date and a short description.
Write the debit account and amount.
Write the credit account and amount.
Check the two amounts match.
Number your entries 1 to 5 and keep them in order.
days.task: Write five journal entries with date, description, debit and credit.
days.title: Journal Entries

days.challenge: Make a trial balance from your books and check it balances.
days.goal: Make a trial balance to check your books.

quiz.explain: A trial balance lists every account with its debit or credit balance, to check the books balance.
options: A list of every account balance to check the books balance
quiz.q: What is a trial balance?

quiz.explain: If debits do not equal credits, there is a mistake to find.
options: There is a mistake to find
quiz.q: What does it mean if a trial balance does not balance?

quiz.explain: Check for a missed entry, a wrong amount, or a debit written as a credit.
options: Check for a missed entry, wrong amount, or swapped debit and credit
quiz.q: How do you find a trial balance error?

steps: List every account from your chart.
For each one, work out its balance from your journal entries.
Put debit balances in one column and credit balances in another.
Add up both columns.
Check the two totals match.
If they do not match, check your entries one by one until you find the error.
days.task: Make a trial balance from your books and confirm debits equal credits.
days.title: The Trial Balance

days.challenge: Work out your profit for last week using sales minus costs.
days.goal: Make an income statement: sales minus costs equals profit.

quiz.explain: An income statement shows sales, costs and profit over a period of time.
options: Sales, costs and profit over a period
quiz.q: What is an income statement?

quiz.explain: Profit equals total income minus total costs.
quiz.q: How do you work out profit?

quiz.explain: The income statement shows a period, like a week or a month. The balance sheet shows one moment in time.
options: The income statement covers a period, the balance sheet shows one moment
The balance sheet covers a period
The income statement shows one moment
quiz.q: How is an income statement different from a balance sheet?

steps: Add up all your sales for the week.
Add up all your costs for the week, grouped by type.
Subtract costs from sales to get your profit or loss.
Write it as a simple statement: sales, minus costs, equals profit.
Check the numbers against your books.
Write one sentence about whether the week was profitable.
days.task: Make an income statement for last week with sales, costs and profit.
days.title: The Income Statement

days.challenge: List everything your business owns and owes today.
days.goal: Make a balance sheet: what you own, what you owe, what is left.

quiz.explain: A balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at one moment in time.
options: Assets, liabilities and equity at one moment
quiz.q: What is a balance sheet?

quiz.explain: Assets are what you own. Liabilities are what you owe. Equity is the difference.
options: Assets are what you own, liabilities what you owe, equity the difference
quiz.q: What goes on a balance sheet?

quiz.explain: Both sides must balance, because of the accounting equation.
quiz.q: Why must a balance sheet balance?

steps: List your assets: cash, bank, stock, equipment.
Add them up for total assets.
List your liabilities: loans and money owed to suppliers.
Add them up for total liabilities.
Work out equity: assets minus liabilities.
Check that assets equal liabilities plus equity.
days.task: Make a balance sheet for today with assets, liabilities and equity.
days.title: The Balance Sheet

days.challenge: Work out if your business had more cash coming in or going out last week.
days.goal: Understand cash flow: money in vs money out.

quiz.explain: Cash flow is the movement of cash in and out of the business.
options: The movement of cash in and out
quiz.q: What is cash flow?

quiz.explain: A business can be profitable on paper but run out of cash if customers pay late.
options: Profit and cash are the same
Profit on paper does not mean cash in hand
quiz.q: Why can a profitable business run out of cash?

quiz.explain: Track cash in and cash out weekly, so you see problems before the money runs out.
options: Track cash weekly to see problems early
quiz.q: How do you keep cash flow healthy?

steps: List all cash that came in last week.
List all cash that went out last week.
Work out the difference: cash in minus cash out.
Check if the result is positive or negative.
Write down why: late payments, big buys, or slow sales.
Write one action to improve cash flow next week.
days.task: Work out last week's cash flow: cash in, cash out, and the difference.
days.title: Cash Flow Basics

video.title: #6 / Putting an Asset on the Balance Sheet

days.challenge: Find one error in your books and fix it properly.
days.goal: Find and fix common bookkeeping errors.

quiz.explain: Common errors are missing entries, wrong amounts, swapped debit and credit, and personal costs mixed in.
options: Missing entries, wrong amounts, swapped sides, mixed personal costs
quiz.q: What are common bookkeeping errors?

quiz.explain: Fix errors with a correcting entry, not by deleting or hiding the mistake.
options: Fix it with a correcting entry
quiz.q: How should you fix an error?

quiz.explain: Regular checks catch errors while they are still small and easy to fix.
options: Regular checks catch errors while small
quiz.q: Why check your books often?

steps: Open your trial balance and check it balances.
Look for a transaction with no receipt.
Look for a personal cost mixed into business costs.
Look for a debit written as a credit.
Fix each error with a clear correcting entry.
Write down what caused each error so it does not happen again.
days.task: Find and fix three errors in your books with correcting entries.
days.title: Fix Common Errors

days.challenge: Produce your income statement and balance sheet from your own books.
days.goal: Produce your first income statement and balance sheet.

project.brief: Produce a real income statement and balance sheet from your own books for the month so far. Both must balance, match your trial balance, and be neat enough to show a business owner.
checks: Income statement made from real numbers
Balance sheet made from real numbers
Receipts filed for the numbers used
Reports are neat enough to show an owner
project.title: Your First Income Statement and Balance Sheet

quiz.explain: A report is only useful if its numbers come from real, checked records.
options: A report is useful only if numbers come from real, checked records
quiz.q: What makes a financial report trustworthy?

quiz.explain: The income statement shows profit over time. The balance sheet shows what you own and owe now.
options: Income statement shows profit over time, balance sheet shows what you own and owe now
quiz.q: What does each report show?

quiz.explain: Checking reports against the trial balance catches errors before the owner sees them.
options: Checking against the trial balance catches errors early
quiz.q: Why check your reports against the trial balance?

steps: Make your trial balance for the month so far.
Make your income statement from the trial balance.
Make your balance sheet from the trial balance.
Check the balance sheet balances.
Check both reports match your receipts.
Present both reports on one page each, neat and clear.
days.task: Produce an income statement and a balance sheet from your books.
days.title: Week 3 Project: Your First Financial Reports

days.challenge: Count your stock today and compare it with your books.
days.goal: Track stock simply: what you have, what you sold, what is left.

quiz.explain: Stock is the goods a business holds to sell.
quiz.q: What is stock?

quiz.explain: Count stock often, because missing stock means lost money or theft.
options: Count often, missing stock means lost money
quiz.q: Why count your stock?

quiz.explain: Stock value is what you paid for it, not what you hope to sell it for.
options: Stock value is what you paid for it
Stock value is the selling price
quiz.q: How do you value your stock?

steps: List every product you hold, with the quantity.
Write what you paid for each one.
Count the real stock on your shelf.
Compare the count with your books.
Write down any difference and why it happened.
Update your books to match the real count.
days.task: Count your stock, compare it with your books, and update the difference.
days.title: Track Stock Simply

days.challenge: Work out the total cost of one worker for one month.
days.goal: Understand payroll basics in plain words.

quiz.explain: Payroll is paying workers: their pay, plus any tax and deductions.
options: Paying workers: pay, tax and deductions
quiz.q: What is payroll?

quiz.explain: A deduction is money taken from pay for tax or other agreed reasons.
options: Money taken from pay for tax or agreed reasons
quiz.q: What is a deduction?

quiz.explain: Payroll records show what was paid, when, and what was taken off, so everyone can check.
options: Payroll records show what was paid, when, and what was taken off
quiz.q: Why keep payroll records?

steps: List everyone who works for the business, even part-time.
Write down each person's pay and how often they are paid.
Work out any tax or deduction for each person.
Write a simple payslip: pay, minus deductions, equals take-home.
Record the payroll in your books as a cost.
Keep a copy of each payslip.
days.task: Make a simple payroll record for one worker with pay, deductions and take-home.
days.title: Payroll Basics

video.title: ACCOUNTING BASICS: Debits and Credits Explained

days.challenge: Make a tax folder with five sections and file one document in each.
days.goal: Keep the tax records a business needs.

quiz.explain: Tax records are the receipts, sales and cost records that prove your numbers to the tax office.
options: Receipts, sales and cost records that prove your numbers
quiz.q: What are tax records?

quiz.explain: Keep tax records for several years, because the tax office can ask for them later.
options: Throw them away at year end
quiz.q: How long should you keep tax records?

quiz.explain: Clean records make tax time fast and calm, instead of a panic.
options: Clean records make tax time fast and calm
Records do not help at tax time
Tax time is always a panic
quiz.q: Why keep clean tax records all year?

steps: Make a tax folder with sections for sales, costs, bank, payroll and receipts.
File this month's records into the right sections.
Write down the tax deadlines for your country or area.
Work out a rough tax amount from your profit so far.
Set aside a small amount for tax each month.
Write down the name of a tax helper or accountant you could ask.
days.task: Set up a tax folder and file this month's records into it.
days.title: Tax Records to Keep

video.title: Complete Accounting Cycle: From Journal Entries to Balance Sheet

days.challenge: Close this month's books in one sitting, step by step.
days.goal: Do a monthly close: finish the month's books properly.

quiz.explain: A monthly close means finishing all entries, reconciling the bank, and making the month's reports.
options: Finishing entries, reconciling the bank, making reports
quiz.q: What is a monthly close?

quiz.explain: A checklist stops you forgetting a step, like the bank reconciliation.
options: A checklist stops you forgetting a step
quiz.q: Why use a monthly close checklist?

quiz.explain: Closing monthly keeps the books fresh and makes year-end easy.
options: Closing monthly keeps books fresh and year-end easy
Monthly closes are too much work
